title: Merging Galaxy Clusters and the Search for New Physics of Dark Matter: A Review
comment: 38 pages, 7 figures: Review accepted for publication in Universe
summary: Merging galaxy clusters represent one of the most powerful macroscopic laboratories in the Universe for searching for new physics within the dark sector. High-velocity cosmic collisions inherently separate the dark matter and stellar components from the highly collisional, X-ray-emitting intracluster gas. These massive systems provide an ideal environment to probe the fundamental nature of dark matter, specifically testing whether it behaves as a strictly collisionless particle or exhibits non-zero self-interactions. While pioneering systems like the Bullet Cluster historically demonstrated the macroscopic decoupling of dark and ordinary matter, the field has evolved into a sophisticated discipline driven by multi-disciplinary methodologies. This review synthesizes recent theoretical and empirical advances in interpreting post-collision dynamics. It examines how the synergy of combined approaches---integrating multi-wavelength observations from gravitational lensing and X-ray mapping with high-fidelity N-body hydrodynamical simulations---allows the translation of macroscopic spatial observables into stringent constraints on microscopic particle properties. Through this synthesis, the work evaluates how leveraging heterogeneous merger ensembles can reliably advance the ongoing search for physics beyond the standard cosmological model.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes recent advances in using merging galaxy clusters as laboratories to probe dark matter self-interactions, integrating multi-wavelength observations (gravitational lensing, X-ray mapping) with N-body hydrodynamical simulations to translate macroscopic spatial observables into constraints on microscopic dark matter particle properties.
AI.motivation: Merging galaxy clusters offer unique natural laboratories to test whether dark matter is strictly collisionless or exhibits self-interactions—a key question for physics beyond the standard cosmological model. The field requires a synthesis of recent theoretical and empirical advances to translate complex post-collision dynamics into meaningful particle physics constraints.
AI.method: The review integrates multi-disciplinary methodologies: multi-wavelength observations from gravitational lensing and X-ray mapping combined with high-fidelity N-body hydrodynamical simulations. It examines how the macroscopic decoupling between dark matter, stellar components, and intracluster gas in mergers can be converted into stringent constraints on microscopic dark matter particle properties, leveraging heterogeneous merger ensembles.
AI.result: The synthesis demonstrates that combined observational and simulation approaches allow translation of macroscopic spatial observables from merging clusters (building on pioneering systems like the Bullet Cluster) into quantitative constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and particle properties.
AI.conclusion: Merging galaxy clusters, analyzed through integrated multi-wavelength and simulation approaches across heterogeneous merger samples, represent a reliable and evolving avenue for probing dark matter self-interactions and searching for physics beyond the standard cosmological model.

title: Spectral Fingerprints Beyond Degeneracies in Primordial Gravitational-Wave Sources
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. We welcome comments and suggestions
summary: Stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds from different primordial mechanisms can produce identical peak frequencies and amplitudes, obscuring their physical origin. We show that the broadband spectral shape breaks this degeneracy. Comparing scalar-induced and gauge-field-induced gravitational waves for identical primordial spectral profiles and cosmological evolution, we find that their spectra retain distinct source-dependent signatures even after matching both the peak frequency and amplitude. While the two mechanisms share a universal deep-infrared behavior, their tensor-source kernels generate different peak morphologies and ultraviolet asymptotic scalings. In particular, the ultraviolet spectrum provides a direct diagnostic of the underlying source mechanism that is insensitive to the overall normalization. Our analysis shows that broadband spectral information contains additional source-dependent signatures that are inaccessible from peak observables alone.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that broadband spectral shape can break the degeneracy between stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds from different primordial production mechanisms (scalar-induced vs. gauge-field-induced), even when their peak frequency and amplitude are identical, by showing that the ultraviolet spectrum provides a direct, normalization-insensitive diagnostic of the underlying source mechanism.
AI.motivation: Stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds from different primordial mechanisms can produce identical peak frequencies and amplitudes, making it difficult to identify their physical origin. This degeneracy obscures the source mechanism behind detected signals, motivating the need for additional observables beyond peak properties.
AI.method: The authors compare scalar-induced and gauge-field-induced gravitational-wave spectra for identical primordial spectral profiles and cosmological evolution. They match both the peak frequency and amplitude between the two mechanisms and analyze how their tensor-source kernels affect the resulting broadband spectral shapes.
AI.result: The two mechanisms share a universal deep-infrared behavior but exhibit distinct peak morphologies and ultraviolet asymptotic scalings. The ultraviolet spectrum serves as a direct diagnostic of the source mechanism that is insensitive to overall normalization, revealing source-dependent signatures not accessible from peak observables alone.
AI.conclusion: Broadband spectral information contains additional source-dependent signatures that break the degeneracy between different primordial gravitational-wave production mechanisms, with the ultraviolet spectral region providing a robust diagnostic of the physical origin.

title: Intrinsic Alignments in Redshift Space I: Symmetries
comment: 43 pages, 9 figures, to be submitted to PRD
summary: Galaxy shapes are unique tensor tracers of large-scale structure, providing a promising avenue to both enhance current cosmological programs and detect new physics beyond the scalar sector. We develop a general formalism to describe the full 3D structure of galaxy shapes and their statistics, including the breaking of isotropy by the line of sight and redshift space distortions. We constructively show that the redshift-space mapping generates a kinematic basis whose form factors are strictly polynomial in the line-of-sight angle $μ= \hat{k} \cdot \hat{n}$, and that parity selection rules restrict scalar-tensor and tensor-tensor correlators to 3 and 13 independent form factors, respectively, with the latter further reduced to 9 by exchange symmetry. We show that this polynomiality is preserved transforming into a total helicity basis denoted by total angular momentum $M$---sourced to be nonzero by powers of the line-of-sight $\hat{n}$---and that this is equivalent to the form factors having spin weights $(1 - μ^2)^{|M|/2}$ and described by associated Legendre polynomials $P^{|M|}_\ell$. We construct estimators for form factors in the normalized total-helicity basis that provide the optimal angular weighting to extract shape information, and connect the full tensor basis to projected shape statistics. To validate our formalism, we study the above tensor form factors within a toy model, showing that all allowed channels are generated even within simplified assumptions, and apply our estimators to halo shape statistics in N-body simulations wherein all channels up to total angular momentum $|M| \leq 2$ are detected. We anticipate that the methods developed here will have applications ranging from optimal extraction of intrinsic-alignments in hydrodynamical simulations to identifying new physics in tensor channels forbidden by selection rules in the standard model of cosmology.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general formalism for describing the full 3D structure of galaxy shapes as tensor tracers of large-scale structure, including parity selection rules, a kinematic basis with polynomial form factors in the line-of-sight angle μ, and a total helicity basis with associated Legendre polynomials. The formalism yields 3 and 13 (reduced to 9) independent form factors for scalar-tensor and tensor-tensor correlators, respectively, with polynomiality preserved under transformation. Optimal estimators are constructed, validated in a toy model and N-body simulations where all channels up to |M| ≤ 2 are detected.
AI.motivation: Galaxy shapes are promising tensor tracers for probing large-scale structure and detecting new physics beyond the scalar sector, but a complete general formalism describing their full 3D statistics—including line-of-sight isotropy breaking and redshift-space distortions—has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors (1) construct a kinematic basis where form factors are strictly polynomial in μ = k̂·n̂ after redshift-space mapping; (2) derive parity selection rules restricting scalar-tensor and tensor-tensor correlators to 3 and 13 independent form factors (9 after exchange symmetry); (3) transform to a total helicity basis labeled by total angular momentum M, where form factors carry spin weights (1−μ²)^|M|/2 and are described by associated Legendre polynomials P^|M|_ℓ; (4) construct optimal estimators in the normalized total-helicity basis; and (5) validate the formalism in a toy model and N-body simulations.
AI.result: All allowed tensor channels are generated even under simplified toy-model assumptions, and in N-body halo shape statistics all channels up to total angular momentum |M| ≤ 2 are detected, confirming the predictive power and practical applicability of the formalism.
AI.conclusion: The developed methods will enable optimal extraction of intrinsic alignments in hydrodynamical simulations and facilitate identifying new physics in tensor channels forbidden by selection rules in the standard cosmological model.

title: Confirmation of the Finch Flatter-Fainter Relation for the Quadruple Images of Lensed Point Sources
comment: 3 pages. Authors' version, including Figure 1 at intended size and full resolution
summary: Finch et al (2002) derived relations for the summed absolute magnifications of quadruply lensed images that vary inversely with flattening in two alternative isothermal gravitational potential models. However, they did not elaborate on the selection effects this "flatter-fainter'' relation induces in actual lensed systems. We test the relation against the Luhtaru et al (2021) sample of 39 quadruply lensed quasars (38 of which we model successfully), using predicted rather than observed magnifications to avoid the complication of microlensing. We found that the summed predicted magnification decreases by a factor of ten over the observed range of flattening.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the "flatter-fainter" relation derived by Finch et al (2002) for quadruply lensed images against a sample of 39 quadruply lensed quasars (38 successfully modeled) from Luhtaru et al (2021). Using predicted rather than observed magnifications to avoid microlensing complications, the authors find that the summed predicted magnification decreases by a factor of ten over the observed range of flattening, confirming the relation and its selection effect.
AI.motivation: Finch et al (2002) derived that summed absolute magnifications of quadruply lensed images vary inversely with flattening in isothermal gravitational potential models, but did not elaborate on the selection effects this "flatter-fainter" relation induces in actual lensed systems. This paper aims to test and quantify these selection effects on real lensed quasar samples.
AI.method: The authors test the flatter-fainter relation against the Luhtaru et al (2021) sample of 39 quadruply lensed quasars (38 successfully modeled), using predicted rather than observed magnifications to avoid the complication of microlensing.
AI.result: The summed predicted magnification decreases by a factor of ten over the observed range of flattening, confirming a strong flatter-fainter selection effect in the sample.
AI.conclusion: The flatter-fainter relation introduces significant selection effects in observed quadruply lensed systems, with flatter systems being systematically fainter—an important consideration for interpreting lensed quasar samples and their biases.

title: A Critical Eddington Ratio for X-Shaped Radio Galaxies
comment: ApJ
summary: We derive a quantitative condition for the formation of X-shaped radio galaxies by evaluating the competition between black hole spin evolution and the radiative fading of relic plasma within our previously proposed framework. The simultaneous visibility of two jet axes requires that the timescale for spin evolution across zero, t_trans, be shorter than the fading timescale of relic radio emission, t_fade. We estimate the transition timescale as t_trans about 5 million /lambda yr, where lambda is the Eddington ratio, and derive a visibility timescale t_fade about equal to 5-20 Myr based on the evolution of the synchrotron break frequency for typical lobe magnetic fields and redshifts. This leads to a critical Eddington ratio lambda_crit in the range 0.3-1, above which systems can exhibit X-shaped morphologies. We show that this threshold naturally produces an environmental dependence, as radiatively efficient accretion is more readily sustained in low-density environments, while feedback in rich clusters tends to drive systems toward radiatively inefficient states with a larger fraction of systems having lambda much less than lambda_crit, suppressing XRG formation. We further demonstrate that the observed low fraction of X-shaped radio galaxies (about 1-5%) arises from the limited overlap window combined with geometric and detectability effects. These results provide a quantitative and testable extension of our previous model, linking X-shaped morphology to accretion rate and environmental conditions through a simple timescale criterion.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a quantitative timescale-based condition for the formation of X-shaped radio galaxies (XRGs), showing that the spin-evolution timescale must be shorter than the relic plasma fading timescale, yielding a critical Eddington ratio threshold of 0.3-1 that naturally explains the environmental dependence and low observed fraction (~1-5%) of these sources.
AI.motivation: To provide a quantitative, testable framework explaining when and why X-shaped radio galaxies form, linking their morphology to accretion physics and environmental conditions through a simple timescale competition criterion.
AI.method: The authors evaluate the competition between black hole spin evolution (transition timescale t_trans ≈ 5 Myr/λ where λ is the Eddington ratio) and the radiative fading of relic plasma (visibility timescale t_fade ≈ 5-20 Myr derived from synchrotron break frequency evolution). They combine these to derive a critical Eddington ratio λ_crit in the range 0.3-1, above which X-shaped morphologies can form.
AI.result: A critical Eddington ratio threshold of 0.3-1 is derived above which XRG formation is possible. The threshold reproduces the observed environmental dependence (radiatively efficient accretion is more common in low-density environments, while feedback in rich clusters suppresses XRG formation) and explains the low observed XRG fraction (~1-5%) through the limited overlap window combined with geometric and detectability effects.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a quantitative extension of the authors' previous model, demonstrating that X-shaped radio galaxy formation can be predicted from accretion rate and environmental conditions via a simple timescale criterion, offering testable predictions.

title: Dark Energy in the $w-c_s^2$ Plane
comment: 21 pages with 3 figures, comments very welcome
summary: We introduce a unified framework for dark energy diagnostics based on the joint phase space of the equation of state $w$ and the sound speed $c_s^2$. The resulting $w-c_s^2$ plane provides a minimal extension beyond background cosmology, capturing both the expansion history and perturbative properties within a single representation. Building on this framework, we define the microphysical flow parameter $F=dc_s^2/dw$, which encodes the dynamical relation between background evolution and perturbative response. We derive a direct connection between the present-day value $F_0$, $H_0$, and $σ_8$, and show that the microphysical flow parameter enables a hierarchy of increasingly stringent consistency tests that substantially reduce the viable dark energy theory space. We further demonstrate how trajectories in the $w-c_s^2$ plane distinguish models that are nearly degenerate at the level of $w(a)$, including canonical quintessence, Chaplygin gas models, and noncanonical scalar field realizations. This framework provides a compact phenomenological bridge between dark energy microphysics and future perturbation-sensitive observations, establishing $F_0$ as a useful discriminator of the kinetic structure underlying cosmic acceleration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified dark energy diagnostic framework based on the joint phase space of the equation of state w and the sound speed c_s^2. The w-c_s^2 plane captures both background expansion and perturbative properties, and the microphysical flow parameter F=dc_s^2/dw encodes the dynamical relation between them. The framework connects F_0 to H_0 and σ_8, enables hierarchical consistency tests that reduce viable dark energy theory space, and distinguishes nearly degenerate models like quintessence, Chaplygin gas, and noncanonical scalar fields.
AI.motivation: Standard background-only diagnostics (e.g., w(a)) are insufficient to distinguish dark energy models that are nearly degenerate at the background level. A framework is needed that simultaneously captures both the expansion history and perturbative properties to discriminate between competing dark energy theories.
AI.method: The authors construct a joint phase space using the equation of state w and sound speed c_s^2, forming the w-c_s^2 plane. They define the microphysical flow parameter F=dc_s^2/dw, derive a direct connection between its present-day value F_0, H_0, and σ_8, and use trajectories in this plane to build a hierarchy of consistency tests for dark energy models.
AI.result: The framework substantially reduces the viable dark energy theory space through increasingly stringent consistency tests. Trajectories in the w-c_s^2 plane successfully distinguish canonical quintessence, Chaplygin gas models, and noncanonical scalar field realizations that are nearly degenerate in w(a). F_0 is established as a useful discriminator of the kinetic structure underlying cosmic acceleration.
AI.conclusion: The w-c_s^2 plane provides a compact phenomenological bridge between dark energy microphysics and future perturbation-sensitive observations, establishing F_0 as a key observable discriminator that connects present-day microphysical flow to H_0 and σ_8.

title: A comprehensive cluster census of Orion. An application of the Significance Mode Analysis (SigMA) algorithm
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures, 6 pages appendix. Submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: Precise astrometric surveys and modern clustering algorithms are working in step to transform our view of star-forming regions. By revealing a much richer substructure than previously accessible, they pave the way for reconstructing star formation histories by accurately resolving and age-dating individual sub-populations. The Orion star-forming complex is the best-studied stellar nursery in the solar neighborhood and the nearest one currently forming massive stars. Even so, a comprehensive characterization of its substructure, including a homogeneous age mapping and extinction analysis, is still incomplete. Here, we present the most complete census of stellar populations across the Orion complex from the newest version of the SigMA algorithm and outline our additions and improvements to the algorithm that have extended its usage to distant (>300 pc) regions. We separate the Orion complex into 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups comprising 11,996 reliable members, with ages ranging from 1.5 to 25 Myr. To evaluate the statistical robustness of each group, we derive cluster persistence values and individual membership probabilities for each source from 10 independent clustering repetitions. Our group memberships agree well with the literature, but SigMA consistently finds a factor of ~2-3 more members. In particular, it resolves more very young populations, such as NGC 2024, RV Orionis, B30, NGC 1977, NGC 2068, and NGC 2071, than previous algorithms. In addition to recovering 28 known clusters and three groups previously classified as substructures, we present 16 new co-eval substructure candidates of the Orion star-forming complex. This work builds up a new high-resolution time-resolved picture of Orion. This spatio-temporal map allows us to relate its stellar content to the surrounding ISM and paves the way for a detailed analysis of its star formation history in the future.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the most complete census of stellar populations in the Orion star-forming complex using an improved version of the SigMA clustering algorithm, identifying 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups with 11,996 members aged 1.5–25 Myr, including 16 new substructure candidates and recovering 28 known clusters.
AI.motivation: While the Orion complex is the nearest and best-studied star-forming region, its substructure characterization—including homogeneous age mapping and extinction analysis—remains incomplete. The authors aim to provide a comprehensive census of stellar populations across the entire complex using improved clustering techniques.
AI.method: The authors extend the SigMA clustering algorithm to work on distant (>300 pc) regions with additions and improvements, then apply it to the entire Orion complex. They derive cluster persistence values and individual membership probabilities from 10 independent clustering repetitions, separating the complex into 47 co-spatial and co-moving stellar groups.
AI.result: SigMA identifies 47 stellar groups comprising 11,996 reliable members with ages from 1.5 to 25 Myr. Memberships agree with literature, but SigMA finds ~2–3 times more members per group, particularly resolving more very young populations (NGC 2024, RV Orionis, B30, NGC 1977, NGC 2068, NGC 2071). The analysis recovers 28 known clusters, three previously classified substructures, and presents 16 new co-eval substructure candidates.
AI.conclusion: This work produces a new high-resolution, time-resolved spatio-temporal map of Orion, enabling the stellar content to be related to the surrounding ISM and laying the groundwork for a detailed future analysis of the region's star formation history.

title: Investigating The Effects of Early Dark Energy on Large-scale Structure Within the EDENS Suite
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures
summary: Early Dark Energy (EDE) models have been suggested as a possible solution to the so-called Hubble Tension, a discrepancy of the measurement of the Hubble constant at early and late times. In this paper, we investigate the effects of EDE on large-scale structure probes of cosmology via the EDENS (Early Dark Energy N-body Simulations) suite. The EDENS suite extends the reach of available EDE simulations considerably by adding volume and resolution. We derive several key metrics, such as the halo mass function, the nonlinear power spectrum, and the concentration-mass relation. Furthermore, we implement a halo occupation distribution model to populate the simulations with synthetic galaxies. This allows us to measure the galaxy-galaxy correlation function and galaxy bias. We choose an EDE model that is consistent with observations across several probes and allows for the increase of the present day value of the Hubble constant to resolve the Hubble tension. This model adds three more parameters to the standard $Λ$CDM model. Additionally, it requires small shifts in the best-fit $Λ$CDM cosmological parameters to accommodate existing observational constraints. We find significant differences between the standard $Λ$CDM model and the EDE model, suggesting that some of our chosen metrics may allow us to distinguish EDE from $Λ$CDM, and future observations should help further constrain possible cosmological models. We release outputs from our simulations via the OpenCosmo data portal.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the EDENS suite of N-body simulations to study the effects of Early Dark Energy (EDE) on large-scale structure. The authors compute halo mass functions, nonlinear power spectra, concentration-mass relations, and use a halo occupation distribution to derive galaxy clustering and bias. They find significant differences from standard ΛCDM that could help distinguish EDE from ΛCDM with future observations, and release their simulation outputs via the OpenCosmo data portal.
AI.motivation: Early Dark Energy models have been proposed as a potential resolution to the Hubble Tension—the discrepancy between early and late-time measurements of the Hubble constant. However, EDE's effects on large-scale structure are not yet well constrained, and existing simulations lack sufficient volume and resolution to probe these effects robustly.
AI.method: The authors develop the EDENS (Early Dark Energy N-body Simulations) suite, which extends the reach of prior EDE simulations in both volume and resolution. They compute key large-scale structure metrics (halo mass function, nonlinear power spectrum, concentration-mass relation) and implement a halo occupation distribution (HOD) model to populate halos with synthetic galaxies, enabling measurements of the galaxy-galaxy correlation function and galaxy bias. The EDE model adds three parameters beyond ΛCDM and uses small shifts in best-fit cosmological parameters to remain consistent with observations.
AI.result: Significant differences are found between the EDE model and standard ΛCDM across the chosen metrics, suggesting that these observables may allow discrimination between EDE and ΛCDM. The simulation outputs are publicly released via the OpenCosmo data portal for further use by the community.
AI.conclusion: The EDENS suite provides a substantial extension of EDE simulation capabilities and demonstrates that EDE leaves measurable imprints on large-scale structure. These differences may permit distinguishing EDE from ΛCDM with future observations, helping to further constrain viable cosmological models addressing the Hubble tension.

title: Interacting stellar winds feeding Sgr A*: from the system of mass-losing stars to the binary IRS 16SW
comment: Proceedings for the IAU Symposium 405: "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time". 5 pages and 2 figures
summary: The discovery of cold structures around Sgr A* has challenged our understanding of the gas dynamics and thermodynamic state of the plasma in its vicinity. This work aims to constrain the conditions for the formation of such structures, namely the cold disc-like structure and the recently discovered G-1-2-3 complex. We conduct hydrodynamic simulations of the observed Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A*. Our simulations show that the plasma chemical composition is crucial for determining the medium properties. We demonstrate that the formation of a cold disc is possible for chemical compositions that are consistent with observational constraints. However, it is not possible to reproduce all the properties of the observed disc which might suggest the interaction with another structure. Additionally, we present our first results on the hydrodynamic modelling of IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary. This is the first step to develop a realistic model on the formation of the G-1-2-3 complex.

AI.tldr: This paper uses hydrodynamic simulations of Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A* to investigate the formation of cold structures (a cold disc and the G-1-2-3 complex). The plasma chemical composition is found to be critical in determining medium properties, and a cold disc can form under observationally consistent compositions, though not all observed properties are reproduced, suggesting interaction with another structure. First results on IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary are also presented as a step toward modeling the G-1-2-3 complex.
AI.motivation: The discovery of cold structures around Sgr A* has challenged existing understanding of gas dynamics and plasma thermodynamics in the Galactic Center, motivating a need to constrain the physical conditions required for their formation.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic simulations of Wolf-Rayet stars feeding Sgr A*, testing various plasma chemical compositions, along with initial hydrodynamic modeling of IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary.
AI.result: Cold disc formation is possible for chemical compositions consistent with observational constraints, but the full set of observed disc properties cannot be reproduced, suggesting interaction with another structure. First results on IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary are reported.
AI.conclusion: The chemical composition of the plasma is a crucial factor in determining medium properties around Sgr A*. A cold disc can form under certain compositions, but additional interactions may be needed to fully explain observations. Modeling IRS 16SW as a colliding-wind binary represents the first step toward a realistic formation model for the G-1-2-3 complex.

title: Dianoga simulations of galaxy clusters and groups: Properties of the baryonic components
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, A&A submitted
summary: We introduce the Dianoga set of cosmological simulations of galaxy clusters and groups, specifically aimed at studying the impact of the implementation of AGN feedback and star formation. Using the OpenGadget3 code, we carry out simulations of 28 regions centred on massive galaxy clusters, and of a cosmological box. This generates a sample of 293 halos with M_{200}> 1.5 x 10^{13} M_{\odot}. Parameters of AGN feedback in the reference implementation were minimally calibrated exclusively to match the local relation between SMBH masses and stellar masses of host galaxies. Simulations are compared to observed galaxy stellar mass function (GSMF), stellar mass fraction in clusters and groups, BCG masses, scaling relations between ICM/IGM properties and profiles of their thermodynamical properties. In the appendix, we show how results vary as we modify the reference feedback model in six alternative configurations. Our reference model predicts a GSMF in general agreement with observations, albeit overestimated in the high end. BCG stellar masses and mass fractions are higher than observed in massive clusters, while being closer to observations for groups. Predicted properties of the ICM/IGM are in general agreement with observations, with the core regions of simulated clusters having entropy and temperature profiles that are slightly less "cool-cored" than observed. A comparison with other implementations of AGN feedback highlights that models including thermal evaporation of the sub-resolution interstellar medium succeed to bring BCG masses and stellar mass fractions closer to observation, and to increase the cool-coreness of simulated clusters. Our results demonstrate that the details of the interface between AGN energy injection and the sub-resolution interstellar medium model are at least as critical as the total feedback efficiency itself.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Dianoga suite of cosmological simulations of galaxy clusters and groups, using the OpenGadget3 code to study the impact of AGN feedback and star formation implementations. The simulations cover 28 massive cluster regions and a cosmological box, yielding 293 halos. The reference AGN feedback model is minimally calibrated to match the local SMBH-mass–stellar-mass relation. Results show general agreement with observed galaxy stellar mass functions and ICM/IGM properties, though BCG masses and mass fractions are overestimated in massive clusters. A key finding is that the interface between AGN energy injection and the sub-resolution interstellar medium model is as critical as total feedback efficiency, with models including thermal evaporation of the ISM producing better agreement with observations.
AI.motivation: To systematically study and quantify how different implementations of AGN feedback and star formation affect the outcomes of cosmological simulations of galaxy clusters and groups, addressing the question of why different feedback prescriptions yield varying predictions and what the critical factors are.
AI.method: The Dianoga suite uses the OpenGadget3 code to simulate 28 regions centered on massive galaxy clusters plus a cosmological box, generating 293 halos with M200 > 1.5×10^13 M_sun. The reference AGN feedback model is minimally calibrated only against the local SMBH–stellar mass relation. Simulations are compared against observed galaxy stellar mass functions, stellar mass fractions, BCG masses, scaling relations, and thermodynamical profiles. Six alternative feedback configurations are explored in an appendix to assess model sensitivity.
AI.result: The reference model produces a galaxy stellar mass function in general agreement with observations (slightly overestimated at the high end), overestimates BCG stellar masses and mass fractions in massive clusters (closer for groups), and predicts ICM/IGM properties broadly consistent with observations though slightly less "cool-cored". Including thermal evaporation of the sub-resolution ISM brings BCG masses and stellar mass fractions closer to observations and increases cool-coreness.
AI.conclusion: The details of how AGN energy is injected and coupled to the sub-resolution interstellar medium model are at least as critical to simulation outcomes as the total feedback efficiency, highlighting the importance of properly modeling the feedback-ISM interface in cosmological simulations.

title: Diverse ionized gas conditions in a dynamically hot, interacting galaxy at $z = 9.31$ revealed by JWST/NIRSpec IFU
comment: Submitted to MNRAS, 12 pages
summary: We present a spatially and spectrally resolved study of an interacting galaxy, Gz9p3 at $z=9.31$, using the James Webb Space Telescope NIRSpec/G395H IFU observation with high-spectral resolution ($R\approx 2700$) mode. Gz9p3 consists of two sub-regions (`core' and `tail'), which show stark contrast in their physical properties. The HII regions in the core are characterized by high electron density ($n_{e}\gtrsim2900$ cm$^{-3}$), low gas-phase metallicity ($0.25$ dex below the mass-metallicity relation), and yet relatively low specific star formation rate (sSFR) among the system. On the other hand, the tail exhibits low electron density ($n_{e}<70$ cm$^{-3}$), relatively high gas-phase metallicity that is consistent with the mass-metallicity relation, and high sSFR. The integrated spectrum thus shows the properties inbetween these two regions. No evidence of ordered rotation in ionized gas is found, suggesting that Gz9p3 is a dynamically hot system. Finally, we find ionized gas outflows characterized by the secondary [OIII]5007 line component throughout most of the system. The outflow velocity is below the escape velocity, making Gz9p3 one of the first galactic systems experiencing a galactic fountain. Overall, our findings indicate that this system is in a phase in which the pristine gas is falling efficiently into the core, diluting the gas metallicity, and enhancing star formation and outflows after the galaxy interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spatially and spectrally resolved study of the interacting galaxy Gz9p3 at z=9.31 using JWST NIRSpec/G395H IFU with high spectral resolution (R≈2700). The galaxy consists of two sub-regions (core and tail) with contrasting properties: the core has high electron density, low metallicity, and low sSFR, while the tail shows low density, higher metallicity, and high sSFR. No ordered rotation is detected (dynamically hot system), and ionized gas outflows below escape velocity suggest a galactic fountain is occurring. The system appears to be in a phase where pristine gas is falling into the core, diluting metallicity and enhancing star formation and outflows after a galaxy interaction.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical conditions, star formation, chemical enrichment, and gas dynamics in one of the earliest interacting galaxies at z=9.31, leveraging JWST's high-resolution IFU capabilities to resolve spatially distinct regions within a single high-redshift galaxy system.
AI.method: JWST NIRSpec/G395H IFU observation at R≈2700, providing spatially and spectrally resolved maps of Gz9p3. The authors analyze two identified sub-regions (core and tail) using emission-line diagnostics including [OIII]5007, measuring electron density, gas-phase metallicity (via mass-metallicity relation offset), specific star formation rate, velocity fields (for rotational signatures), and outflow properties via secondary line components.
AI.result: The core shows high electron density (ne≳2900 cm⁻³), low metallicity (0.25 dex below mass-metallicity relation), and low sSFR. The tail shows low density (ne<70 cm⁻³), metallicity consistent with the mass-metallicity relation, and high sSFR. The system is dynamically hot (no ordered rotation detected), and ionized gas outflows with velocities below escape velocity are found throughout most of the system, indicating a galactic fountain.
AI.conclusion: Gz9p3 is undergoing an interaction-driven phase where pristine gas efficiently falls into the core, diluting metallicity and triggering star formation and outflows. It represents one of the first galactic systems observed experiencing a galactic fountain, providing insight into early galaxy assembly and feedback processes at z≈9.

title: A stochastic forward model for the intergalactic dispersion-measure distribution of Fast Radio Bursts
summary: Fast Radio Bursts probe ionised baryons through their observed dispersion measures. We present \turbofrb, a semi-analytic stochastic forward model for the intergalactic dispersion-measure distribution, $P({\rm DM}_{\rm IGM}\mid z)$, that resolves the diffuse IGM, halo, and filament contributions as explicit physical channels, with the halo and filament encounter rates coupled by a latent line-of-sight environmental variable. Only four effective parameters are calibrated against hydrodynamical ray-traced IllustrisTNG benchmark. The model matches the benchmark mean DM to the percent level and yields a per-redshift Jensen-Shannon divergence of at most $5\times10^{-3}$ across $z = 0.5$-$2.5$. The per-sightline channel decomposition makes explicit what closed-form parametric descriptions cannot show: the diffuse IGM sets the body of the distribution, while halos and filaments populate the high-DM tail. Applied to representative localised FRBs, the forward likelihood quantifies host-excess events independently of their astrophysical signatures and recovers the injected $H_0$ within $1σ$ in a closed-loop consistency test. The \turbofrb package is available at \href{https://github.com/jefersonfortunato/turbofrb}{github.com/jefersonfortunato/turbofrb}.

AI.tldr: This paper presents turbofrb, a semi-analytic stochastic forward model for the intergalactic dispersion-measure distribution of Fast Radio Bursts, resolving diffuse IGM, halo, and filament contributions as explicit physical channels. Calibrated against IllustrisTNG simulations with only four effective parameters, it matches benchmark mean DM to percent level and is used for cosmological inference including H0 recovery.
AI.motivation: FRBs probe ionised baryons through dispersion measures, but closed-form parametric descriptions cannot explicitly resolve the separate contributions from the diffuse IGM, halos, and filaments along a sightline. A forward model that decomposes these channels is needed to better interpret DM distributions and enable robust cosmological inference.
AI.method: The model is a semi-analytic stochastic forward model for P(DM_IGM|z) that treats halo and filament encounter rates as coupled to a latent line-of-sight environmental variable. Only four effective parameters are calibrated against hydrodynamical ray-traced IllustrisTNG benchmark simulations.
AI.result: The model matches the benchmark mean DM to the percent level and achieves a per-redshift Jensen-Shannon divergence of at most 5×10^-3 across z = 0.5-2.5. The per-sightline decomposition shows the diffuse IGM sets the distribution body while halos and filaments populate the high-DM tail. Applied to localised FRBs, it quantifies host-excess events and recovers injected H0 within 1σ in a closed-loop test.
AI.conclusion: The explicit channel decomposition in turbofrb provides physical interpretability beyond closed-form parametric models, enables host-excess quantification independent of astrophysical signatures, and serves as a validated forward model for FRB-based cosmological inference.

title: The VariableTNG project: Unveiling the physical drivers of galaxy quenching
comment: Total: 18 pages, 12 main text + 5 appendixs. 14 figures, 8 main text + 6 appendix
summary: Understanding the physical processes that regulate galaxy quenching is a key challenge in galaxy formation and evolution. The VariableTNG (VTNG) project provides a laboratory to investigate these processes, as it systematically varies eight parameters of galaxy formation while keeping the initial conditions fixed, allowing the effects of individual feedback prescriptions to be isolated. We use interpretable machine-learning techniques as a tool to identify the parameters that most strongly regulate the quenched galaxy fraction. Our goal is to quantify the relative importance of the galaxy formation and feedback parameters that regulate the quenched galaxy fraction at z=0, determine how their influence changes across stellar mass and environment. We compute the quenched galaxy fraction for 26 VTNG boxes as a function of stellar mass, black hole mass, and gas mass, considering both the total galaxy population and separate samples of central and satellite galaxies. We train Random Forest regressors to predict the variation of the quenched fraction relative to the TNG100-1 model and use SHAP values to quantify both the magnitude and direction of the influence of each parameter. Our analysis reveals that only a small subset of the VTNG parameters dominates the variance of the quenched fraction. The stellar feedback wind parameter is the primary driver at low stellar masses, while its importance gradually shifts toward AGN-related parameters at higher masses. The supernova temperature also plays an important role at both extremes of the stellar-mass range. This transition persists when the galaxy population is divided into central and satellite systems. Comparisons with observational measurements further suggest that variations in these feedback parameters may contribute to the discrepancies between the fiducial TNG100-1 model and the observed passive galaxy population.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the VariableTNG (VTNG) simulation suite—which varies eight galaxy formation parameters with fixed initial conditions—combined with interpretable machine learning (Random Forest + SHAP values) to identify which physical parameters most strongly regulate the quenched galaxy fraction at z=0, revealing that stellar feedback winds dominate at low stellar masses while AGN-related parameters dominate at high masses.
AI.motivation: Understanding the physical processes regulating galaxy quenching is a key challenge in galaxy formation and evolution. The VTNG project provides a laboratory to isolate the effects of individual feedback prescriptions by systematically varying eight parameters while keeping initial conditions fixed. The goal is to quantify the relative importance of galaxy formation and feedback parameters regulating the quenched fraction and how their influence changes across stellar mass and environment, potentially explaining discrepancies between the fiducial TNG100-1 model and observations.
AI.method: Quenched galaxy fractions are computed for 26 VTNG boxes as functions of stellar mass, black hole mass, and gas mass, for total, central, and satellite galaxy populations. Random Forest regressors are trained to predict quenched fraction variations relative to the TNG100-1 fiducial model, and SHAP values are used to quantify the magnitude and direction of influence of each varied parameter.
AI.result: Only a small subset of VTNG parameters dominates the variance of the quenched fraction. The stellar feedback wind parameter is the primary driver at low stellar masses, with importance shifting toward AGN-related parameters at higher masses. The supernova temperature also plays an important role at both extremes of the stellar-mass range. This transition persists for both central and satellite galaxy samples. Comparisons with observations suggest these feedback parameter variations may contribute to discrepancies between the fiducial TNG100-1 model and observed passive galaxy population.
AI.conclusion: The stellar-to-AGN feedback transition in governing galaxy quenching is robust across galaxy sub-populations, and interpretable ML applied to controlled simulation suites like VTNG provides a powerful framework to identify dominant physical regulators. Variations in the key feedback parameters may explain part of the mismatch between simulated and observed passive galaxy populations.

title: Infrared Lines from Sterile-Neutrino Transition Magnetic Moments at JWST
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: We investigate infrared line signatures from radiatively decaying sterile-neutrino dark matter using publicly available JWST/NIRSpec IFU blank-sky observations. The main signal considered is the sterile-to-sterile transition $N_1\to N_2γ$, induced by the transition magnetic dipole coefficient $d_{NNγ}$, with $m_1>m_2$. In contrast to ordinary two-photon decays of axion-like or Majoron-like particles, the observed photon energy is not fixed by the full dark matter mass, but by the small mass splitting $Δm=m_1-m_2$. Thus, a keV-scale sterile-neutrino dark matter state can generate an eV-scale infrared photon line in the JWST band. We construct a $χ^2$-based line-search analysis using the NIRSpec IFU $\rm F170LP$-$\rm G235M$ blank-sky data toward $\rm GN\text{-}z11$, modelling the smooth continuum with a cubic spline and including the Milky Way halo decay flux. In the absence of a significant excess, we derive projected limits on $d_{NNγ}$ and on the decay width $Γ_{N_1\to N_2γ}$ for $0.1~{\rm eV}\lesssimΔm\lesssim1~{\rm eV}$. For a sterile component saturating the dark matter abundance, the strongest sensitivity reaches $d_{NNγ}\lesssim7\times10^{-14}~{\rm GeV}^{-1}$ and $Γ_{N_1\to N_2γ}\lesssim10^{-25}~{\rm s}^{-1}$. We also include a minimal anomalous-Majoron benchmark, $ω\toγγ$, obtaining JWST sensitivity to $λ_{ωγγ}\sim10^{-11}$-$10^{-9}~{\rm GeV}^{-1}$ for $m_ω\sim0.6$-$1~{\rm eV}$.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes JWST/NIRSpec IFU blank-sky observations toward GN-z11 to search for infrared line signatures from radiatively decaying sterile-neutrino dark matter, specifically the transition N1→N2γ induced by the magnetic dipole coefficient dNNγ. Since the emitted photon energy depends on the mass splitting Δm rather than the full dark matter mass, keV-scale sterile neutrinos can produce eV-scale infrared lines detectable by JWST. Using a χ²-based line search, they find no significant excess and derive projected limits of dNNγ≲7×10⁻¹⁴ GeV⁻¹ and Γ≲10⁻²⁵ s⁻¹ for Δm between 0.1-1 eV, plus sensitivity to anomalous Majoron decay ω→γγ.
AI.motivation: To probe the radiative decay of sterile-neutrino dark matter into infrared photons, exploiting the fact that the photon energy is set by the small mass splitting (Δm) between two sterile states rather than the full keV-scale mass, thereby bringing the signal into the JWST observational band.
AI.method: Utilizes public JWST/NIRSpec IFU F170LP-G235M blank-sky observations toward GN-z11. Constructs a χ²-based line-search analysis, models the smooth continuum with a cubic spline, includes Milky Way halo decay flux, and searches for a photon line from the N1→N2γ transition.
AI.result: No significant line excess is found. Derived projected upper limits on dNNγ and ΓN1→N2γ for Δm in the range 0.1-1 eV. For a sterile component saturating the dark matter abundance, the strongest sensitivity reaches dNNγ≲7×10⁻¹⁴ GeV⁻¹ and Γ≲10⁻²⁵ s⁻¹. Also, for an anomalous Majoron benchmark ω→γγ, JWST is sensitive to λωγγ~10⁻¹¹-10⁻⁹ GeV⁻¹ for mω~0.6-1 eV.
AI.conclusion: JWST NIRSpec observations provide a new and competitive probe of sterile-neutrino dark matter radiative transitions in the infrared, with constraints that are complementary to traditional keV-scale X-ray searches. The technique also extends to other exotic light dark-sector particles such as anomalous Majorons.

title: Measuring Simulated Circumgalactic Medium Turbulence with Emission-Weighted Projected Velocity Structure Functions in FOGGIE
comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: The spatially-resolved kinematics of line emission from the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of a galaxy can contain information about the CGM turbulence, which may play an important role in galaxy evolution. Due to the region's diffuse nature, there have been limited observations of low-redshift CGM emission until recent efforts that use spatially-resolved emission line kinematics to probe CGM turbulence. We use velocity structure functions (VSFs) as a measure for the properties of turbulence using the high-resolution cosmological zoom-in FOGGIE simulations. We focus on the location of the "turnover" in the VSF slope, often used as a measurement of the turbulence driving scale, and study how resolution, measurement area size, projection effects, and gas temperature influence the inferred CGM turbulence driving scale. We find that projection significantly lowers the VSF normalization but we do not find significant differences in the slope between 3D VSFs and emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs. We find that the size of the area used to measure the VSF, which can be thought of as the size of the emission nebula for a given instrument sensitivity, correlates directly with the turnover location in the VSF. These dependencies should be considered when using VSFs to interpret CGM turbulence from emission data, as projection, resolution and sensitivity constraints, and the temperature of the gas probed will all have a measurable effect on the VSF structure and the corresponding inferred turbulent properties.

AI.tldr: This paper uses FOGGIE cosmological zoom-in simulations to study velocity structure functions (VSFs) as a probe of CGM turbulence, finding that projection reduces VSF normalization without significantly changing slope, while the measurement area size directly correlates with the VSF turnover location (turbulence driving scale).
AI.motivation: The CGM plays an important role in galaxy evolution, and its turbulence can be probed through spatially-resolved line emission kinematics. However, limited observations exist due to the diffuse nature of the CGM, and the reliability of the inferred turbulence driving scale from VSFs as a function of observational and resolution effects needs investigation.
AI.method: The authors use high-resolution cosmological zoom-in FOGGIE simulations and compute velocity structure functions (VSFs) to measure turbulence properties in the CGM. They systematically investigate how resolution, measurement area size, projection effects (3D vs. emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs), and gas temperature influence the inferred turbulence driving scale, identified as the VSF slope turnover location.
AI.result: Projection significantly lowers the VSF normalization but does not substantially change the slope between 3D VSFs and emission-weighted projected 2D VSFs. The size of the measurement area (related to the emission nebula size for a given instrument sensitivity) correlates directly with the VSF turnover location.
AI.conclusion: When using VSFs to interpret CGM turbulence from emission data, one must account for projection, resolution and sensitivity constraints, and the gas temperature probed, as all measurably affect the VSF structure and the inferred turbulent properties.

title: Large eROSITA X-ray sources as 2MRS galaxy groups
comment: 12 pages, A&A in press
summary: We aim to exploit the large area coverage, good sensitivity, and low instrumental background of eROSITA to detect the faint surface brightness emission of galaxy groups from the Two Micron All Sky Survey Redshift Survey (2MRS). Using the data from eROSITA-DE Data Release 1, including images, exposure maps, and local background maps, we performed a wavelet decomposition of image mosaics in the 0.6--2.3 keV band at angular scales of 1/8-16'. We adopted 8-16' scales for source detection and 2-4' scales to improve catalog purity. A novel identification method based on the ranked partial Hausdorff distance fully exploits the X-ray image and group membership information. Random catalogs were used to control match purity, and the identification threshold was chosen to maximize the catalog size at a fixed purity. {We present a catalog of 619 X-ray galaxy groups with 80% purity, and define subsamples with 90% and 97% purity. Bright sources closely match the AXES-2MRS catalog (which is based on ROSAT All Sky Survey data analysis on spatial scales of 12-24'). The X-ray luminosity function of our groups agrees with previous studies down to 5.e41 erg/s. Using dynamical mass estimates, we find that the X-ray counterpart completeness for groups with >=4 members exceeds 60% for masses >2e13 Msun. We modeled the 2MRS group catalog and justify the inclusion of two-member groups in the identification. This study demonstrates that large X-ray sources on spatial scales relevant for cosmological studies of baryonic distributions can be reliably detected and identified using nearby galaxy group catalogs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a catalog of 619 X-ray galaxy groups detected by eROSITA-DE Data Release 1, using wavelet decomposition of images in the 0.6-2.3 keV band and a novel identification method based on ranked partial Hausdorff distance against 2MRS groups. The catalog achieves 80% purity (with 90% and 97% purity subsamples), agrees with previous ROSAT-based results, and demonstrates reliable detection of large-scale X-ray emission down to luminosities of 5×10^41 erg/s and masses above 2×10^13 Msun.
AI.motivation: To exploit eROSITA's large area coverage, good sensitivity, and low instrumental background to detect faint surface brightness X-ray emission from nearby galaxy groups, which had been difficult with previous surveys.
AI.method: Wavelet decomposition of eROSITA-DE DR1 image mosaics in the 0.6-2.3 keV band at angular scales of 1/8 to 16 arcminutes, using 8-16' scales for source detection and 2-4' scales for catalog purity improvement. Identification used a ranked partial Hausdorff distance method, with random catalogs controlling match purity and thresholds optimized for catalog size at fixed purity. Dynamical mass estimates were used to assess completeness.
AI.result: A catalog of 619 X-ray galaxy groups at 80% purity, with 90% and 97% purity subsamples. Bright sources match the AXES-2MRS catalog. The X-ray luminosity function agrees with previous studies down to 5×10^41 erg/s. X-ray counterpart completeness exceeds 60% for groups with ≥4 members and masses >2×10^13 Msun.
AI.conclusion: Large X-ray sources on spatial scales relevant for cosmological studies of baryonic distributions can be reliably detected and identified using nearby galaxy group catalogs, demonstrating eROSITA's capability for this science.

title: The VariableTNG project: how baryonic mechanisms shape galaxy properties
summary: We use 50 Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations, varying eight subgrid parameters at fixed cosmology and initial conditions, to determine which baryonic processes regulate galaxies and black holes at $z=6$ and $z=8$. We compare the simulations with recent high-redshift measurements of the stellar mass function, star-forming main sequence, stellar and gas-phase mass-metallicity relations, stellar mass-size relation, and black-hole host and accretion properties. The simulations reproduce several broad trends in these observables, although differences remain in gas-phase metallicity, galaxy size, and the most extreme black-hole populations. Given the substantial uncertainties in both the physical modelling and the observational inference of high-redshift galaxy properties, we regard these differences as diagnostic tensions rather than definitive model failures. Random-forest analyses reveal a clear hierarchy in parameter sensitivity. The abundance of low-mass galaxies is regulated primarily by stellar feedback, particularly the supernova temperature $T_{\mathrm{SN}}$ and thermal wind fraction $τ_{\mathrm{w}}$, whereas the sensitivity of the scatter in the star-forming main sequence is weaker and redshift dependent. The high-accretion tail of black-hole growth depends on black-hole seeding and feedback parameters, but also on $T_{\mathrm{SN}}$, suggesting that stellar feedback indirectly regulates rapid black-hole growth through its impact on the available gas supply. Although cosmic variance can obscure these intrinsic responses in independent small volumes, our controlled experiment identifies stellar feedback as a common physical link between early low-mass galaxy formation and rapid black-hole growth.

AI.tldr: Using 50 Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations varying eight subgrid parameters, the paper examines which baryonic processes regulate galaxies and black holes at z=6 and z=8 by comparing against high-redshift observations. Random-forest analyses identify stellar feedback (especially supernova temperature and thermal wind fraction) as the primary regulator of low-mass galaxy abundance and an indirect regulator of rapid black-hole growth via gas supply.
AI.motivation: To determine which baryonic processes govern early galaxy formation and black-hole growth at z=6 and z=8, given substantial uncertainties in high-redshift physical modeling and observational inference.
AI.method: Fifty Sobol-sampled VariableTNG simulations varying eight subgrid parameters at fixed cosmology and initial conditions, compared against high-redshift observations (stellar mass function, star-forming main sequence, mass-metallicity relations, size relation, black-hole properties), with random-forest analyses to quantify parameter sensitivity hierarchies.
AI.result: Simulations reproduce broad observational trends but show differences in gas-phase metallicity, galaxy size, and extreme black-hole populations. Stellar feedback (supernova temperature and thermal wind fraction) dominates low-mass galaxy regulation; the high-accretion black-hole tail depends on seeding/feedback parameters and stellar feedback, indicating indirect regulation via gas supply.
AI.conclusion: Stellar feedback is a common physical link connecting early low-mass galaxy formation and rapid black-hole growth, though cosmic variance can obscure these intrinsic responses in independent small volumes.

title: Imprints of Mass Accretion History on Galaxy Cluster Morphology
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures
summary: Variations in dynamical states of galaxy clusters can introduce biases and scatter in observable-mass relations. The dynamical state of a cluster is an emergent feature of its mass accretion history (MAH), it is therefore useful to constrain the MAH of the cluster. In this work, we characterize 305 massive clusters from The300 project by connecting features from their projected stellar distributions to their mass accretion histories (MAH). As a baseline, we first correlate host dark matter halo dynamical state indicators at $z=0$ with their MAH via the Spearman rank correlation coefficient $ρ_{\mathrm{sp}}$. Both substructure mass fraction and center-of-mass offset measurements correlate strongly with the MAH measured between $0.1\lesssim z\lesssim 1$. We repeat this exercise with morphological measurements of projected stellar density maps, many of which exhibit moderate correlation strength with different times in the MAH. Broadly, core morphological measurements ($r \leq 30\,\mathrm{kpc}$) correlate better with early-time MAH. Core-excised ($50\,\mathrm{kpc} \leq r \leq 1\,\mathrm{Mpc}$) morphological measurements correlate better with late-time MAH. We further quantify the MAH prediction power of both traditional dynamical state indicators and morphological parameters using Multivariable Conditional Abundance Matching (MultiCAM). MultiCAM employs simple rank-ordering operations, making it straightforward to translate to observed datasets. We find reasonable ($ρ_{\mathrm{sp}} \geq 0.6$) performance for predictions of the mass fraction between $1\lesssim z\lesssim 0.1$, though with notable information loss when using projected quantities. In one example application of our methodology, we use the coefficients of the MultiCAM models to select subsamples of galaxy clusters that have accreted more (or less) of their $z = 0$ mass budget over a given time frame.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes 305 massive galaxy clusters from The300 project by linking projected stellar distribution features to their mass accretion histories (MAH). The authors first correlate halo dynamical state indicators with MAH, then examine morphological measurements of projected stellar density maps. They find core morphological features correlate with early-time MAH while core-excised features correlate with late-time MAH. Using Multivariable Conditional Abundance Matching (MultiCAM), they achieve reasonable MAH prediction performance (ρ_sp ≥ 0.6) for mass fractions between 1 ≲ z ≲ 0.1, and apply the method to select cluster subsamples based on accretion history.
AI.motivation: Dynamical states of galaxy clusters can introduce biases and scatter in observable-mass relations, and the dynamical state is an emergent property of the cluster's mass accretion history. Constraining the MAH is therefore useful for improving cluster mass calibration and understanding cluster evolution.
AI.method: The authors use 305 massive clusters from The300 project, correlating host dark matter halo dynamical state indicators (substructure mass fraction, center-of-mass offset) with MAH using Spearman rank correlation. They analyze morphological measurements of projected stellar density maps, separating core (r ≤ 30 kpc) and core-excised (50 kpc ≤ r ≤ 1 Mpc) regimes. They then apply Multivariable Conditional Abundance Matching (MultiCAM), a simple rank-ordering technique, to predict MAH from observables.
AI.result: Traditional dynamical state indicators correlate strongly with MAH between 0.1 ≲ z ≲ 1. Core morphological measurements correlate better with early-time MAH, while core-excised measurements correlate better with late-time MAH. MultiCAM achieves reasonable prediction performance (ρ_sp ≥ 0.6) for mass fraction predictions between 1 ≲ z ≲ 0.1, though with some information loss when using projected quantities.
AI.conclusion: Projected stellar distribution features can serve as useful proxies for constraining galaxy cluster mass accretion histories. MultiCAM provides a straightforward, rank-ordering-based framework applicable to observed datasets, enabling selection of cluster subsamples with specific accretion characteristics.

title: Diffuse Dwarf Galaxies in Galaxy Clusters: I. Stellar Populations and Radial Gradients
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We use Keck/KCWI spectroscopy to study one ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) and five Nearly-UDGs (NUDGEs) in the Perseus cluster, together with an additional UDG in the Coma cluster. As the first paper in a series, we focus on the global and radial stellar population properties of our sample. We find that these galaxies host intermediate-to old stellar populations, with typical ages of ~7 Gyr, low metallicities ([M/H]$\simeq$ -0.9 dex), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] abundances (~0.3 dex), consistent with previous studies. Six galaxies lie within the scatter of the present-day mass-metallicity relation (MZR), whereas the Coma UDG (DF11) is more consistent with the MZR of high-z galaxies (z ~ 2). We find no strong correlation between global stellar population properties and cluster infall parameters, suggesting that any environmental impact is not easily traceable through integrated stellar populations. We go one step further and measure radial gradients for three galaxies. Two show flat age and mildly negative metallicity gradients, similar to classical dwarfs, while one shows a rising metallicity profile as recently found in other UDGs. Comparing with classical dwarfs, we find a continuous correlation between metallicity gradient and globular cluster (GC) richness, where more GC-rich systems tend to show rising profiles. We propose that preferential tidal disruption of GCs in the inner regions of galaxies naturally produces rising metallicity profiles, unlike GC-poor classical dwarfs. This mechanism, potentially coupled with strong stellar feedback from early concentrated star formation, may explain the unusual rising metallicity profiles observed in GC-rich UDGs/NUDGEs.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Keck/KCWI spectroscopy to study the stellar populations of six ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) and nearly-UDGs in the Perseus and Coma clusters. They find intermediate-to-old ages (~7 Gyr), low metallicities ([M/H]~-0.9), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] (~0.3), with most galaxies following the local mass-metallicity relation. Radial gradients for three galaxies show flat age profiles and varied metallicity gradients, with a correlation between metallicity gradient and globular cluster richness. They propose tidal disruption of inner GCs and strong stellar feedback as mechanisms producing rising metallicity profiles in GC-rich UDGs.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and evolution of ultra-diffuse galaxies by measuring their global and radial stellar population properties, and to investigate how environment and globular cluster content influence their chemical evolution.
AI.method: Keck/KCWI spectroscopic observations of six UDG/NUDGE galaxies in the Perseus cluster and one UDG in the Coma cluster, measuring global stellar population parameters (age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe]) and radial gradients for three galaxies, correlated with cluster infall parameters and globular cluster richness.
AI.result: Galaxies show intermediate-to-old ages (~7 Gyr), low metallicities ([M/H]~-0.9 dex), and enhanced [Mg/Fe] (~0.3 dex). Six galaxies follow the local MZR while the Coma UDG (DF11) resembles high-z galaxies. No strong correlation with cluster infall parameters. Radial gradients reveal flat age and mildly negative metallicity gradients for two galaxies, while one shows a rising metallicity profile. A continuous correlation exists between metallicity gradient and GC richness.
AI.conclusion: Rising metallicity profiles in GC-rich UDGs/NUDGEs can be explained by preferential tidal disruption of inner globular clusters, potentially coupled with strong stellar feedback from early concentrated star formation, distinguishing them from GC-poor classical dwarfs.

title: eROSITA cosmology with galaxy groups: hot gas budget out to the virial radius
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Non-gravitational processes that expel hot gas beyond the virial regions of groups and clusters of galaxies, known collectively as baryonic feedback, play a key role in reshaping the matter distribution of the Universe on Mpc scales. We use eROSITA observations of a complete sample of 25 galaxy groups selected from the first public release of the eROSITA-DE data (eRASS1) and identified with the Two Micron Redshift Survey optical group catalogue (2MRS). We extract and fit surface brightness (SBx) profiles and present hot gas mass and hot gas fraction profiles out to $R_{200}$. We perform a Bayesian analysis of $M_{\mathrm{gas}}-M_{\mathrm{tot}}$, $L_{\mathrm{X}}-M_{\mathrm{tot}}$, and $L_{\mathrm{X}}-M_{\mathrm{gas}}$ relations, taking into account the aperture covariance effects. At $R_{500}$, we report uniformly flat SBx profiles with a mean $β$ parameter of $0.38 \pm0.04$, steepening to $β= 0.76\pm0.19$ beyond $R_{500}$. We measure a sub-cosmic hot gas fraction at the median mass of our sample $M_{500} = 2.54\times10^{13}M_{\odot}$ of $ f_{\mathrm{gas,500}} = 4.32\pm0.42\%$. Similarly, at $R_{200}$ and the median mass $M_{\mathrm{ 200}} = 3.69\times10^{13}M_{\odot}$, we obtain $f_{\mathrm{gas,200}}=5.78\pm0.69\%$. Our $f_{\mathrm{gas}}-M_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{X}}-M_{\mathrm{tot}}$ relations show significant deviations from the predictions of the strong feedback variants of the FLAMINGO simulation ($2.5σ$ to $8.0σ$ tension), while fiducial FLAMINGO and BAHAMAS provide the closest match to our measurements. Using our measured baryon fractions and the \texttt{SP(k)} model, we infer a $10\%-15\%$ reduction in the matter power spectrum at $k = 5\ h\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ relative to a dark matter-only universe, in agreement with fiducial FLAMINGO and BAHAMAS, while revealing a growing tension on smaller scales with the strong feedback variants.

AI.tldr: Using eROSITA observations of 25 galaxy groups from eRASS1 matched to the 2MRS optical catalogue, the authors measure hot gas profiles out to R200, derive gas fractions and scaling relations, and find that the data favor fiducial FLAMINGO and BAHAMAS simulations over strong-feedback variants, implying a 10–15% suppression of the matter power spectrum at k=5 h/Mpc relative to dark matter-only predictions.
AI.motivation: Baryonic feedback processes that expel hot gas beyond virial regions significantly reshape the matter distribution on Mpc scales. It is crucial to quantify these effects observationally to constrain feedback models and correct cosmological inferences from weak lensing and other probes.
AI.method: The authors extract and fit surface brightness profiles from eROSITA observations of a complete sample of 25 galaxy groups from eRASS1 (matched to 2MRS), deriving hot gas mass and fraction profiles out to R200. They perform Bayesian fits of M_gas–M_tot, L_X–M_tot, and L_X–M_gas relations with aperture covariance handling, and compare against FLAMINGO and BAHAMAS simulations.
AI.result: Flat surface brightness profiles at R500 (β=0.38±0.04) steepening beyond R500 (β=0.76±0.19). Sub-cosmic hot gas fractions: f_gas,500=4.32±0.42% at M500=2.54e13 Msun and f_gas,200=5.78±0.69% at M200=3.69e13 Msun. Scaling relations show 2.5σ–8.0σ tension with strong-feedback FLAMINGO variants, while fiducial FLAMINGO and BAHAMAS match best. A 10–15% power spectrum suppression at k=5 h/Mpc is inferred, with growing tension on smaller scales for strong-feedback models.
AI.conclusion: Observations of galaxy group hot gas distributions from eROSITA favor moderate baryonic feedback (fiducial FLAMINGO, BAHAMAS) over strong-feedback variants, implying a significant but bounded suppression of the matter power spectrum on non-linear scales due to baryonic processes.

title: Candidates for the most [$O_{III}$] $\lambda5007$-luminous planetary nebula in the Milky Way. I. Integrated light properties of NGC 6572, NGC 6884, and M 1-71
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, accepted in A&A
summary: The bright-end cutoff of the planetary nebula luminosity function (PNLF) serves as an extragalactic standard candle. However, the physical properties of planetary nebulae (PNe) at the PNLF cutoff have been studied only in nearby galaxies, where the PNe appear mostly as point sources. Galactic PNLF is further poorly constrained, primarily due to uncertainties in Galactic PN distances. Following a recent Galactic PNLF survey based on Gaia distances, we aim to characterise PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff. We observed three PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff using the Potsdam Multi-Aperture Spectrophotometer (PMAS). We determined their chemical abundances and constructed photoionisation models to derive the central star luminosity (L) and effective temperature (Teff). We constrained the central star masses and most likely distances consistent with the prediction of stellar evolution models. Using these distances, we determined the absolute magnitude M5007. PNe of our sample are located within the top 1 mag of the Galactic PNLF (-4.20 < M5007 <-3.60), with similar nebular properties and a narrow progenitor mass range (1.30-1.75 Msolar). The measured extinction is mostly dominated by the foreground Galactic extinction. The trend between the circum-nebular extinction and central star mass of our PNe is in agreement with those derived in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and M31. All PNe in our sample exhibit weak-emission line star (wels) features in their spectra, but we confirmed that some of these lines originate from the nebula. The PNe are similar in terms of their nebular properties and evolutionary stage. Their characteristics are also consistent with the most [OIII]5007-luminous PNe in the LMC and M31. We demonstrate the importance of circum-nebular extinction and the initial-final mass relation (IFMR) to understand the universality of PNLF as a standard candle.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes three planetary nebula (PN) candidates located at the bright-end cutoff of the Galactic planetary nebula luminosity function (PNLF) using PMAS spectrophotometry and photoionization modeling. The PNe have absolute magnitudes between -4.20 and -3.60, similar nebular properties, and progenitor masses of 1.30-1.75 M☉. They show weak-emission line star (wels) features and are consistent with the most [OIII]5007-luminous PNe in the LMC and M31. The study highlights the roles of circum-nebular extinction and the initial-final mass relation (IFMR) in understanding the PNLF universality.
AI.motivation: The PNLF bright-end cutoff is a standard extragalactic distance indicator, but physical properties of PNe at this cutoff have only been characterized in nearby galaxies as unresolved point sources. Galactic PNLF PNe have remained poorly constrained due to distance uncertainties. This work aims to characterize PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff using recent Gaia-based distances.
AI.method: Observations of three PN candidates at the Galactic PNLF cutoff were made using the Potsdam Multi-Aperture Spectrophotometer (PMAS). Chemical abundances were determined, and photoionization models were constructed to derive central star luminosity and effective temperature. Central star masses and most likely distances were constrained from stellar evolution model predictions, enabling determination of absolute magnitudes M5007.
AI.result: The sample PNe lie within the top 1 mag of the Galactic PNLF (-4.20 < M5007 < -3.60), share similar nebular properties, and have a narrow progenitor mass range of 1.30-1.75 M☉. Foreground Galactic extinction dominates the measured extinction. Circum-nebular extinction trends against central star mass agree with LMC and M31 results. All PNe exhibit wels features (some lines confirmed from the nebula), and their characteristics are consistent with the most [OIII]5007-luminous PNe in the LMC and M31.
AI.conclusion: The Galactic PNLF cutoff PNe are similar to each other in nebular properties and evolutionary stage, matching the most luminous PNe in the LMC and M31. Circum-nebular extinction and the initial-final mass relation (IFMR) are demonstrated to be important for understanding the universality of the PNLF as a standard candle.

title: $R_{\rm e}$, or not $R_{\rm e}$: Developing $R_5\equiv R_{-2}$ as a scale radius for galaxy sizes, masses, and mass-to-light ratios
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to MNRAS. Companion Python package R5Tools available at https://github.com/A-Graham/R5Tools
summary: The effective half-light radius $R_{\rm e}$ marks an arbitrary 50-per-cent light boundary, and scaling relations involving such effective radii and their associated surface brightnesses, $μ_{\rm e}$, depend systematically on the adopted percentage. Here, a gradient-defined scale, $R_5\equiv R_{-2}$, is developed as an alternative. It is the projected radius where the logarithmic slope of the intensity profile is equal to $-2$, corresponding to a slope of the surface-brightness profile of $5.00\,\text{mag dex}^{-1}$, and the radius at which the luminosity contributed per logarithmic radial interval is maximal. It can be measured non-parametrically or with a parametrized fit. For the Sérsic $R^{1/n}$ family, the exact relation $R_5=(2n/b_n)^n\,R_{\rm e}$ is derived, with $R_5/R_{\rm e}\rightarrow{\rm e}^{1/6}\approx1.181$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Reparameterizing the (now $b_n$-free) $R^{1/n}$ model in terms of the observable pair $(R_5,μ_5)$ removes the non-linear (radial scale)-(concentration, $n$) coupling and because the local slope is $5\,\text{mag dex}^{-1}$ at $R_5$, correlated measurement errors in $R_5$ and $μ_5$ largely cancel when deriving the inferred total magnitude. Additionally, an exact single-integral identity is provided to relate any projected light fraction to the fraction within a sphere of the same radius. The directly observable $R_5$ is connected, through a weakly $n$-dependent factor, to the anisotropy-insensitive intrinsic radius $r_{-3}$, yielding a refined $n$-dependent Wolf-type mass estimator $M_{-3}$ and spatial mass-to-light ratio $(M_{\rm dyn}/L)_{-3}$. Past half-light substitutions in dynamical mass estimators have introduced systematic concentration-dependent offsets of 12-18 per~cent in enclosed mass and a range $>20$ per~cent in the mass-to-light ratio. Dynamical mass estimators for (dark matter)-free stellar systems are also provided.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes replacing the arbitrary 50% half-light radius (R_e) with a gradient-defined scale R_5 (the radius where the intensity profile's logarithmic slope is -2) for galaxy scaling relations and dynamical mass estimators. This scale has exact analytic relations to Sérsic parameters, decouples radial scale from concentration, reduces correlated measurement errors, and improves dynamical mass estimates by removing systematic concentration-dependent biases of 12-18%.
AI.motivation: The effective half-light radius is an arbitrary choice (50% light boundary), causing scaling relations and dynamical mass estimates to depend systematically on the adopted percentage. This introduces concentration-dependent biases in mass estimators and creates nonlinear couplings between fitted parameters that complicate measurement and interpretation.
AI.method: The authors define R_5 as the projected radius where the logarithmic slope of the intensity profile equals -2 (surface-brightness slope of 5.00 mag/dex).
